::: {.lead}
Two weeks before the release of *Rooftop Rescue*, Salma, the producer,
finds a folder called "found stuff": a rain sound from a website, a cute
drawing of a cat, a famous pop song for the trailer, a font "free for
personal use", and old piano music. "Can we use all this?" asks Tariq. "It
was all free on the Internet!" In this lesson you learn who **owns** such
media and when you may use it: **intellectual property**, **copyright**,
**licences** and the limits of **fair use**. Then you learn to **use**
licensed and open assets well: where to find them, how to keep their
licences, how to write credits with **TASL**, and how to check every asset
before the release. This lesson explains the basics; it is not legal advice,
and the laws differ from country to country. Every section ends with a short
task. Seminar 12 practises all of it on the assets of a game.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary intellectual-property copyright copyright-holder public-domain work-for-hire licence creative-commons attribution fair-use takedown-notice open-asset tasl credits-file rights-clearance >}}

## 12.1 What is protected, and who owns it?

A game is full of creations of the mind: art, music, code, a name and a
logo. The law protects them as **intellectual property**. Games also learn
from each other, so a team must know where inspiration ends and copying
begins (@fig-inspired).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.1 — Intellectual property (IP)"}
**Intellectual property** is the protection of creations of the mind, so
that their owners control how they are used. In game media, two kinds
matter most:

- **Copyright:** art, music, sound, video, stories and code.
- **Trademark:** names, logos and signs that show who made a product.

**Ideas, genres and mechanics** (a cat hero, a rain level, a jump) are free
to use. The **expression** is protected: the actual drawings, sprites,
music, text and code.
:::

![Inspired by, or copied?](images/inspired-copied.png){#fig-inspired width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.1 — Two close calls"}
1. Nour traced a sprite from another game "to save time" and changed the
   colours: this is copying. Nour draws a new sprite.
2. The new logo looks like the logo of a big drink brand: a trademark
   problem. Salma asks for a new design with a different shape and colours.
3. The rain level looks like rain levels in many games: an idea, so it
   stays.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"I changed 30 % of it, so it is mine." There is no percentage rule. If the
original can still be recognized, you need permission.
:::

### Who owns it, and for how long?

Copyright is the kind of IP that media makers meet every day
(@fig-copyright).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.2 — Copyright and its owner"}
**Copyright** gives the **copyright holder** the right to decide who may
**copy**, **share**, **change** and **show** a work.

- It starts **automatically** when the work is made: no form, no © sign.
- It lasts a long time: in many countries until 70 years after the
  creator's death. Then the work is in the **public domain**: anyone may
  use it.
- **Employees:** their work for the studio usually belongs to the studio
  (**work for hire**). **Freelancers** keep the copyright, unless a
  **written contract** gives it to the studio. A **library** keeps it and
  gives the studio a licence. **Fan art** uses the studio's characters, so
  the studio decides what fans may do with it.
:::

![What the copyright holder decides.](images/copyright-rights.png){#fig-copyright width=94%}

![Who owns the assets of Rooftop Rescue?](images/ownership.png){#fig-owner width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.2 — The theme and the piano piece"}
1. A freelance composer wrote the theme music. Night Owl paid, but there
   is **no written contract**, so the composer still owns it. Salma sends a
   short contract, and both sign before the release.
2. The old piano piece is by a composer who died in 1900: it has been in
   the **public domain** for a long time.
3. A recording by a famous pianist has its own copyright. So Yara records
   the piece on the studio piano, and the recording belongs to Night Owl.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"There is no © sign, so it is free." Copyright needs no sign. Without a
licence, every work is **all rights reserved**. And "we paid for it" does
not move the copyright: the contract decides.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Inspired or copied?"}
Decide for each, with a reason: (a) a puzzle game with falling blocks;
(b) a game that uses the exact music of a famous film; (c) a hero in a
blue cap drawn in your own style; (d) a title with the name of a famous
character of another company.

*Your result:* four decisions with reasons.

::: {.check}
(a) Inspired: a genre and a mechanic are free. (b) Copied: the music is
the expression, so it needs a licence. (c) Inspired: your own drawing of
an idea. (d) A trademark problem: the name belongs to the other company.
:::
:::

## 12.2 Licences: Creative Commons, and a licence to keep

To use a work that someone else owns, you need a **licence**
(@fig-spectrum).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.3 — Licences"}
A **licence** is permission from the copyright holder, with conditions.

- **All rights reserved:** ask the holder for permission.
- **A paid licence:** for example from a music or sound library. A
  **royalty-free** licence is paid once and does not mean free of
  copyright.
- **Creative Commons** licences are standard licences with parts: **BY**
  (give credit), **SA** (share changes alike), **NC** (non-commercial
  only), **ND** (no changes). **CC0** gives the work to the public domain.
- **Attribution (credit):** the creator, the title, the source and the
  licence.
:::

![From all rights reserved to the public domain.](images/licence-spectrum.png){#fig-spectrum width=94%}

![Creative Commons: four conditions.](images/cc-licences.png){#fig-cc width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.3 — Three assets in the folder"}
1. The **rain sound** is CC BY: Night Owl may use it in the game it sells,
   with a credit.
2. The **cat drawing** is CC BY-NC: not for a game that is sold. Salma
   writes to the artist and asks for a paid licence.
3. The **font** is "free for personal use": a game for sale is commercial
   use, so Night Owl buys a commercial licence.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/licence-lab.html" poster="sims/licence-lab.png" title="Licence Lab: what may Night Owl do?" height="600" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reading only "Creative Commons" and not the parts. CC BY and CC BY-NC look
similar, but one allows a game for sale and the other does not.
:::

### Read and save the licence

Before you download, read the licence page (@fig-page).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.4 — Reading a licence page"}
Check five things:

1. **The author** (a person or a studio, not the website).
2. **The exact licence** and its version, for example CC BY 4.0.
3. **Commercial use** and **changes**: allowed or not?
4. **The credit** the author asks for.
5. Other limits, such as "do not sell the file alone".

Then **save** the page (as a PDF with the date) or the licence file in the
project. Licences on a website can change later; your saved copy shows what
you agreed to.
:::

![Reading a licence page (example).](images/licence-page.png){#fig-page width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.4 — Night Rain"}
1. Author: Lina Haddad. Licence: CC BY 4.0.
2. Commercial use: yes. Changes: yes. Credit: yes.
3. Yara shortens the loop to 20 s and saves the page as
   `licences/night_rain.pdf`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reading only the word "free". "Free" can mean free of cost but not free to
use in a game for sale. The licence decides.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Read the licence"}
1. In **Licence Lab**, build CC BY, CC BY-NC, CC BY-ND and CC BY-SA.
2. For each, write in one line what Night Owl may do in *Rooftop Rescue*.

*Your result:* four lines.

::: {.check}
CC BY: use and change it in the game for sale, with a credit. CC BY-NC: not
in a game that is sold (ask for a paid licence). CC BY-ND: use it only
unchanged, with a credit. CC BY-SA: use and change it, with a credit, but
share the changed work under the same licence.
:::
:::

## 12.3 Fair use, and when something goes wrong

Some laws allow limited use without permission: **fair use** or **fair
dealing** (@fig-fair). It is narrow, so a studio plans with licences, and
it knows what to do when a problem comes.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.5 — Fair use and takedown notices"}
- **Fair use** (in some countries **fair dealing**) allows limited use of
  a work without permission, for example for **criticism, review,
  teaching, news or parody**. A court looks at the purpose, the kind of
  work, the amount used, and the effect on the market. There is **no fixed
  number** of seconds that is always fine.
- A **takedown notice** asks a store or a website to remove content that
  uses a work without permission. React fast: remove or replace the asset,
  and answer.
- **Images and sounds made with an AI tool:** the terms of the tool and the
  law decide the use, and they change. Record the tool and the prompt, and
  say honestly how the asset was made.
:::

![Fair use: questions a court asks.](images/fair-use.png){#fig-fair width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.5 — Eight seconds of a famous film"}
1. Tariq wants 8 seconds of a famous film in the promo clip: "It is short,
   so it is fair use."
2. But the purpose is to **sell** a game, and the film is a creative work.
3. Salma decides: no film clip. Tariq uses gameplay shots of *Rooftop
   Rescue* instead.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"Under 10 seconds is always fair use", "I wrote 'no copyright intended'",
or ignoring a takedown notice. None of these protects the studio. For a
game that is sold, plan with **licences**.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Fair or not?"}
Decide for each and give one reason: (a) a teacher shows a 20-second clip
of a game in class to discuss its camera; (b) a studio puts a famous song
in its trailer; (c) a reviewer shows short gameplay clips in a video that
criticizes the game.

*Your result:* three decisions with reasons.

::: {.check}
(a) Likely fair use: teaching, a short part, no market harm. (b) Not fair
use: the trailer sells a game, so the song needs a licence. (c) Likely fair
use: criticism and review with short clips.
:::
:::

## 12.4 Using assets: sources, credits and the check

A game's assets come from five kinds of sources, and each needs a different
proof (@fig-sources).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.6 — Sources of assets"}
- **Own work:** made by the team (employees: work for hire).
- **Open asset sites:** **open assets** under CC0, CC BY, CC BY-SA or the
  OFL.
- **Paid asset libraries** and stores: usually a **royalty-free** licence;
  keep the receipt and the licence text.
- **Public domain** archives: old works whose copyright has ended, and CC0.
- **Freelancers:** work made on order, with a signed contract.

"Found with an image search" is not a source: it does not tell you who owns
the work or under which licence.
:::

![Where assets can come from.](images/asset-sources.png){#fig-sources width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.6 — Four new assets"}
1. A thunder sound from an open sound site, CC BY 4.0.
2. A roof-tile pack from an art site, CC BY-SA 4.0.
3. A pixel font from a font site, SIL Open Font License.
4. Theme music from a freelancer, with a signed contract.

For each, Salma saves the licence page in the project folder `licences/`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Trusting a re-upload. An asset that someone copied to another site under a
"free" label may not be theirs to share. Download from the creator's own
page or a known library.
:::

### Credits with TASL

A correct credit has four parts: **TASL** (@fig-tasl).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.7 — TASL credits"}
- **T**itle: the name of the work.
- **A**uthor: the creator.
- **S**ource: where it can be found (a link).
- **L**icence: the licence, with a link if possible.

Add the **changes** you made, for example "shortened by Yara". Write each
credit in the **credits screen** of the game and in the **credits file** of
the project (@fig-credits).
:::

![A credit with TASL.](images/tasl.png){#fig-tasl width=94%}

![The credits screen and the credits file.](images/credits.png){#fig-credits width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.7 — Three credits"}
1. "Night Rain" by Lina Haddad, sounds.example.org/night-rain, CC BY 4.0,
   shortened to 20 s.
2. "Roof Tiles Pack" by Karim Art, art.example.net/roof-tiles, CC BY-SA
   4.0, recoloured by Nour (the recoloured tiles are also CC BY-SA 4.0).
3. "Roof Sans" by Omar Studio, fonts.example.com/roof-sans, SIL OFL 1.1.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/credit-builder.html" poster="sims/credit-builder.png" title="Credit Builder: TASL for Rooftop Rescue" height="720" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"Sounds from the Internet" as a credit. It names no title, no author and no
licence. Every asset gets its own TASL line.
:::

### Check every asset before the release

Before a game goes to the store, the team checks **every** asset, also the
store page and the trailer (@fig-check).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.8 — The rights check"}
Ask five questions for each asset: **1** Who made it? **2** Who owns it?
**3** Which licence? **4** Does our use fit the licence? **5** Is the
credit written? Then give the asset a **status**:

- **cleared:** all five answers are "yes";
- **to fix:** one thing is missing, such as a credit or a contract;
- **replace:** the source is unknown, or the licence does not allow our
  use.
:::

![A rights check.](images/rights-check.png){#fig-check width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.8 — Four assets of Rooftop Rescue"}
1. The thunder sound: CC BY, the credit is written: **cleared**.
2. The theme music: a freelancer, paid, but no contract: **to fix** (sign
   a contract).
3. A cloud photo from an image search, page unknown: **replace**.
4. A pixel font under the SIL Open Font License, no credit yet: **to fix**
   (write the credit).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Checking only the game files. The store page, the trailer and the
marketing images are public too: check them as well.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your credits file"}
1. In **Credit Builder**, build the three credits.
2. Start a credits file for your two assets: asset file, title, author,
   source, licence, changes, saved licence file.

*Your result:* a credits file with two entries.

::: {.check}
Credit Builder: "Night Rain" by Lina Haddad, sounds.example.org, CC BY 4.0,
shortened to 20 s; "Roof Tiles Pack" by Karim Art, CC BY-SA 4.0,
recoloured by Nour; "Roof Sans" by Omar Studio, SIL OFL 1.1. Your file has
one TASL line for each of your two assets.
:::
:::
## Case study: Can We Use It?

Salma checks the "found stuff" folder: a rain sound under CC BY, a cat
drawing under CC BY-NC, piano music by a composer who died in 1900 and
recorded by Yara, a famous pop song with "no copyright intended" in its
description, a font "free for personal use", and 8 seconds of a famous
film for the promo. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses
these assets. In the mini-game below you decide what Night Owl Games may do
with each one.

## Further reading

Schell, *The Art of Game Design*, 3rd ed., the chapters on the team and on
the game's documents. Creative Commons, "About CC licenses" and "Recommended
practices for attribution" (creativecommons.org). SIL International, "SIL
Open Font License" (openfontlicense.org).

## Exercises

1. What is intellectual property? Name the two kinds that matter most for game media.
2. Does copyright protect the idea "a cat on a roof"? Explain.
3. Who owns a drawing that an employee made for the studio? And music by a freelancer without a contract?
4. Explain BY, SA, NC and ND in one line each.
5. Why is fair use a poor plan for a game's trailer?
6. Why is "found with an image search" not a source?
7. Why should you save the licence page?
8. What do the letters TASL stand for?
9. Write a TASL credit for a photo "Old Roofs" by Sara Nader, photos.example.org/old-roofs, CC BY 4.0.
10. A sound has an unknown source. Which status does it get in the rights check?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. The protection of creations of the mind; copyright and trademark.
2. No: copyright protects the expression (a concrete drawing), not the idea.
3. The studio (work for hire); the freelancer keeps it.
4. BY: give credit; SA: share changes under the same licence; NC: no commercial use; ND: no changes.
5. Fair use is narrow and decided case by case; a trailer sells a game, so it needs licences.
6. It does not say who owns the work or under which licence.
7. Licences on websites can change; the saved copy shows what you agreed to.
8. Title, author, source, licence.
9. "Old Roofs" by Sara Nader, photos.example.org/old-roofs, CC BY 4.0.
10. Replace.
:::
